lessons.title: Letters and expressions
lessons.summary: Read what a letter stands for and write simple expressions from everyday quantities.
lessons.objective: Read what a letter stands for and write simple expressions from everyday quantities.
lessons.before: Recall the order of operations and how to multiply signed numbers.
lessons.ideas:
Write \(3n\) for three copies of \(n\). The coefficient counts the copies.

Seven less than \(x\) is \(x-7\).

For four copies of \(a+3\), write \(4(a+3)\).
lessons.method:
What can a letter represent?

A letter can stand for a quantity that changes. If one bag contains n items, another bag with the same contents also has n items.

Where do I start with a difference?

Start from the quantity named after 'less than'. Then take away the stated amount.

When does a group need brackets?

Work out what belongs to one group first. When there are several copies, the multiplication must apply to the whole group.
mistakes: An expression gives a rule that works for different values of the letter.
Read the words back from your expression to check the order.
Keeping brackets links the fixed and changing parts of the same group.

examples.title: Write repeated groups and the extra items
examples.question: There are 4 bags with \(n\) counters in each bag, plus 5 loose counters. Write an expression for the total.
examples.solution:
Multiply the number of bags, 4, by the number of counters in each bag, \(n\).

The loose counters add \(5\) to the product.

The expression is \(4n+5\).

examples.title: Write a difference in the stated order
examples.question: Write an expression for 6 less than a number \(x\).
examples.solution:
Start from the named number. 'Less than' tells you how much to take away.

Subtract \(6\) from \(x\).

The expression is \(x-6\).

examples.title: Use brackets for the full group
examples.question: A print shop makes 8 packs. Each pack contains \(a\) large cards and 6 small cards. Write an expression for the total number of cards.
examples.solution:
One complete pack contains both sizes of card. Add the part that varies to the fixed number.

Multiply one full pack, \(a+6\), by \(8\). Use brackets to keep the two sizes together.

The expression is \(8(a+6)\).

lessons.title: Substitution with one letter
lessons.summary: Replace one letter with a given value, including negatives and fractions.
lessons.objective: Replace one letter with a given value, including negatives and fractions.
lessons.before: Recall the order of operations and how to multiply signed numbers.
lessons.ideas:
If \(x=7\), then \(2x+5\) becomes \(2\times7+5\).

The base in \((-4)^2\) is the whole number \(-4\).

Multiply or divide before adding or subtracting unless brackets change the order.
lessons.method:
What does substituting a value mean?

Replace the letter everywhere it appears. Keep the operations in the rule unchanged.

What changes when the number is negative?

Write brackets around the value before raising it to a power or subtracting it.

How do I substitute a fraction?

Put the fraction where the letter was. Read the operations outside the fraction afterwards.
mistakes: Side-by-side coefficient and letter mean multiply.
The negative sign is part of the value you substitute.
A coefficient multiplies the entire substituted fraction.

examples.title: Evaluate a rule with one input
examples.question: Find the value of \(6x+8\) when \(x=4\).
examples.solution:
Replace \(x\) with \(4\) to get \(6\times 4+8\).

Multiply first, then add \(8\).

The answer is \(32\).

examples.title: Square a substituted negative value
examples.question: Find the value of \(x^2-8\) when \(x=-5\).
examples.solution:
Put the entire negative value in brackets: \((-5)^2-8\).

The square is \(25\) because both factors are negative. Subtract \(8\) after squaring.

The answer is \(17\).

examples.title: Substitute a fraction and follow the operation order
examples.question: Evaluate \(7p+6\) when \(p=\frac{1}{6}\). Give an exact value.
examples.solution:
Replace \(p\) by \(\frac{1}{6}\). Multiply it by \(7\).

Then add \(6\) to the product \(\frac{7}{6}\).

The answer is \(\frac{43}{6}\).

lessons.title: Using formulae with several letters
lessons.summary: Match each value to its letter, follow the order of operations and include the requested unit.
lessons.objective: Match each value to its letter, follow the order of operations and include the requested unit.
lessons.before: Recall the order of operations and how to multiply signed numbers.
lessons.ideas:
Substitute the given number for each occurrence of the matching letter.

Only multiply the part of the formula that contains the variable being replaced.

Preserve brackets and fraction bars when replacing values.
lessons.method:
Which number belongs in which place?

Read the given values with their letters. Mark each letter before filling in its value.

Which value changes and which stays fixed?

Read the sentence that defines each letter. For a cost rule, a fixed fee can appear as a separate term.

What happens above and below the fraction bar?

The fraction bar separates two groups. Work out the value of each group before dividing.
mistakes: Two different letters can represent different values.
A fixed part of the rule is counted once.
Dividing one part of the numerator separately changes the formula.

examples.title: Keep the values with the right letters
examples.question: Evaluate \(5a-b\) for \(a=4\) and \(b=-6\).
examples.solution:
Replace both letters: \(5\times4-(-6)\).

The product is \(20\). Subtracting the negative value is addition.

The answer is \(26\).

examples.title: Use a formula to find a total cost
examples.question: A workshop charges \(C=6+5n\) pounds for \(n\) tickets. Find the total cost when the group buys 7 tickets.
examples.solution:
Put \(7\) in place of \(n\). The fixed amount \(6\) stays the same.

The ticket cost is \(5\times7=35\). Add the fixed charge.

The answer is \(41\).

examples.title: Replace all the letters in a fraction formula
examples.question: Each tray has mass \(w\) kg. Use \(w=\frac{M-b}{n}\), where \(M\) is the combined mass of the trays and their crate, \(b\) is the crate mass and \(n\) is the number of identical trays. Find \(w\) when \(M=34\), \(b=7\) and \(n=6\). Give an exact value in kilograms.
examples.solution:
Put the combined mass and crate mass above the division bar, and the count below it.

The tray mass without its crate is \(34-7=27\). Then divide by \(6\).

The answer is \(\frac{9}{2}\).

  2. A workshop charges \(C=9+8n\) pounds for \(n\) tickets. Find the total cost when the group buys 4 tickets.

    Show your working.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put the combined mass and crate mass above the division bar, and the count below it.

The tray mass without its crate is \(472-9=463\). Then divide by \(5\).

The answer is \(\frac{463}{5}\).

(b)

Put \(4\) in place of \(n\). The fixed amount \(9\) stays the same.

The ticket cost is \(8\times4=32\). Add the fixed charge.

The answer is \(41\).

(a)

Finish the full numerator before dividing by the number of trays.

(b)

The fixed charge is paid once. Multiply only the charge per ticket.
